summary: Describes an LDAP extended operation that reverses the roles of client and server for the rest of a session, or lets each peer act as both. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: You called the librarian and asked questions. Now you swap, and the librarian asks you.

questions: swap ldap client and server roles
what is the ldap turn operation
how do i reverse client and server roles in ldap
subtitle: An LDAP extension that lets a connection flip so the original client becomes the server, or lets both sides act as both.

tldr.problem: LDAP normally has the client open the connection to the server, but sometimes the server side needs to be the one that starts the connection. Designing new server-initiated sessions would mean inventing new security mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: A Turn extended operation, sent after the connection is up, reverses the client and server roles for the rest of the session, or optionally makes both peers able to act as both.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol and the RFC itself says its security implications are not fully studied. It has since been updated by RFC 8996.

facts.label: Response
facts.value: ExtendedResponse with no responseName or responseValue

today: RFC 4531 is an Experimental protocol and has been updated by RFC 8996. It was never an Internet standard of any kind, and it says the security implications of its design are not fully studied.

sections.title: Why Reverse the Roles
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is a client-server protocol that usually runs over a reliable octet-stream such as TCP. Normally the client connects to the server's listener at a well-known address.

Sometimes it is better for the server to start the stream. The RFC notes that one could write a whole new specification for server-initiated LDAP sessions, but that would require new authentication and other security mechanisms. Instead, this document adds the Turn operation, which reverses the client-server roles so the peer that opened the connection becomes the server.

Turn can also be used so that both peers act in both roles. That is useful when both peers are directory servers that want to ask each other, as LDAP clients, to perform operations, for example in replicated or distributed setups. The operation is meant for peers that already have a mutual agreement, made outside the protocol, that calls for this.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the caller asks and the answerer replies. Turn lets them trade places on the same call, so nobody has to hang up and redial.

sections.title: The Turn Request and Response
sections.content:
Turn is an LDAP extended operation identified by the OID 1.3.6.1.1.19. The request is an ExtendedRequest whose requestValue is a BER-encoded turnValue: a SEQUENCE with a BOOLEAN mutual field (default FALSE) and an identifier field of type LDAPString.

If mutual is TRUE, both peers may act as both client and server. If it is FALSE, the roles are simply reversed. The identifier is a locally defined policy identifier, typically tied to the mutual agreement the turn is part of.

The response is an ExtendedResponse with no responseName or responseValue. A resultCode of success is returned if and only if the responder is willing and able to turn the session as requested. Otherwise a different result code comes back.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a note saying 'let us swap, and here is the code word for our deal'. The answer is just yes, or a no with a reason.

sections.title: Authentication After a Turn
sections.content:
Each peer is authenticated separately in each of its roles. After the turn, the responding peer, now in its client role, has an anonymous association at the initiating peer, now in its server role. It can establish its identity by requesting and completing a Bind operation.

If the turn was mutual, the initiating peer's earlier authentication as a client at the responding peer is left intact. If the turn was not mutual, that association is void.

The RFC walks through three scenarios: StartTLS followed by a Simple bind, StartTLS followed by SASL EXTERNAL, and a SASL mechanism that gives mutual authentication (such as GSSAPI) followed by an EXTERNAL bind after the turn. In each, the original client authenticates, sends Turn(TRUE, "XXYYZ"), gets a success response, and then the original server binds as the new client.
sections.plainLanguage: After swapping, the new asker has to show who they are again. The old proof only counts for the old job.

sections.title: Security Layers and Cautions
sections.content:
Turn does not change how LDAP, SASL and TLS layer together, and it does not remove the general restriction against multiple TLS layers or multiple SASL layers. If a TLS layer is already installed, StartTLS must fail. After TLS is set up, the peer that started the LDAP session (the original client) performs the server identity check, treating itself as the client and its peer as the server, whichever peer asked for TLS.

The RFC is frank about risk. Reversing roles likely introduces security considerations the authors did not foresee, and the implications of the authentication and data security models are not fully studied. It hopes experimentation will lead to a better understanding.

  • Process LDAP, SASL, TLS and other events in the right roles. Turn reverses roles in LDAP and in SASL exchanges, but not within the TLS layer or the transport connection.
  • The responding server should restrict Turn to authorized clients. Knowing a valid identifier should not be the only factor.
  • Where TLS is expected, start it before the Turn and before any Bind.
sections.plainLanguage: Swapping jobs is a bit risky, so check who is asking, lock the door first, and do not trust a secret code word alone.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned the LDAP Object Identifier 1.3.6.1.1.19 to identify the LDAP Turn Operation, and registered an LDAP Protocol Mechanism entry with the same OID, described as an Extended Operation. Both name RFC 4531 as the specification and the author as change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: The Turn operation got its own official number so everyone can recognize it.
